Between 2019 and 2020, EI programs in RI reported a 33% average of staff turnover, with the highest turnover for Early Interventionist I (the lowest paid position in EI).
Due to the shortage of qualified applicants for Early Interventionist II positions, programs in RI such as Meeting Street are offering signing bonus to recruit applicants.
In terms of overall need for these services, there was an 88% delay or interruption of services to children due to staff turnover and shortages, as well as 88% of families withdrawing from EI services due to staff challenges and turnover in 2021 (RI KidsCount, 2021).
This shortage of qualified early intervention personnel places children in Rhode Island at higher risk for developing delays and/or disabilities.
Studies indicate that the severe staff shortage has made it difficult for Early Intervention programs to accept all children in need of help (Nesi & Sherman, 2022).
In terms of state competition, Rhode Island College currently offers two options: a master’s degree in Early Childhood Special Education and an Early Intervention Certificate program.

The master program includes course work designed to enhance specific knowledge of Early Intervention: a course on working with families in EI, and a required internship in EI.
Other course work addresses develop and assessment of young children (birth through age 8) with special needs.
The inclusion of EI related courses in the Masters was designed to increase skills and interest relative to EI.
However, pay scales differences between public educational systems and EI programs appear to dampen enthusiasm for the EI jobs.
RIC’s EI certificate is designed and limited to current EI employees who have at least two years in EI and are seeking to advance in EI.
In contrast, the URI Certificate in Early Intervention is targeted to undergraduates and therefore does not conflict with either RIC programs instead, it creates an additional pathway to become qualified personnel in EI.
The only regional competitor is Northeastern University.
Northeastern offers a Certificate in Early Intervention, with coursework similar to URI’s EI certificate proposal, that the state of Massachusetts has approved for provisional certification with advanced standing (PCAS) in Early Intervention.

Applicants who possess the PCAS must then complete 1440 hours of supervised employment in an EI setting before applying for permanent standing.
It is likely that the proposed certificate in EI at URI would allow graduates to obtain this provisional certification in Massachusetts.

Service and Community Life Committee Report #2024-2025-01 April 10, 2025 Faculty Senate Meeting Constitutional Amendment to Appendix B of the University Manual, Article III, “Membership” Rationale: The University of Rhode Island’s Retired Faculty Association (‘RFA’) is recognized by the office of the President and the Provost as the official representative of faculty members who have retired from the University of Rhode Island.
The RFA is housed within the office of the Provost and recently authored URI’s “Retired Faculty Handbook”.
Many RFA members are interested in remaining active on campus and contributing their time and talents to assist current faculty.
As part of that involvement, the RFA has requested their organization be represented on the Faculty Senate by an ex officio member (the RFA president or, if unavailable, their designee).
As with other ex officio members, this person would have the right to make and second motions but would not be able to vote.
This provides the RFA a voice in academic and organizational matters while maintaining the current policy that only active faculty elected as Senators shall be accorded the right to vote in Faculty Senate meetings.

Procedurally, according to Section 1 of Article VII of the Faculty Senate Constitution (“Amendment of the Constitution”), a majority vote of the total voting membership of the Faculty Senate is required to approve the measure.
The matter must then be ratified by the affirmative vote of two-thirds of the General Faculty voting on the question (i.e a subsequent referendum of the General Faculty is required for approval).
Existing Language: Appendix B Article III – Membership “1.
The Senate shall consist of designated ex officio members and of elected members of the General faculty, chosen in the approximate ratio of one senator for each 12 full-time faculty members, or a minimum of two senators.
In the case of colleges with five or fewer senators, at least half of the senators shall be tenure-track faculty.
In the case of colleges with six or more senators, at least two-thirds of the senators shall be tenure-track faculty.
Any member of the tenure-track faculty with the rank of professor, associate professor, assistant professor, or instructor may be elected a member of the Senate.

Any member of the General Faculty with the rank or title of clinical professor, associate clinical professor, research professor, associate research professor, teaching professor, or associate teaching professor and who has had a full-time academic appointment at the University for a minimum of five continuous years may be elected a member of the Senate.
The Senate will provide means by which all eligible faculty members not in a college or the library have the opportunity to vote and to be candidates for election.
The President, the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs, the Vice Provosts, the Vice Presidents, the deans of the colleges and schools, the Dean of Admissions, the person who served as Senate President during the previous academic year, the current Student Senate President or, in the absence of that person, a designee member of the Student Senate, and the President of the Graduate Student Association or, in the absence of that person, the Vice President of the Graduate Student Association shall be members of the Senate ex officio without the right to vote, but with the right to make and second motions.
